This project outlines the architecture and implementation of a search engine, detailing its core components, technologies, data flow, and underlying rationale.
1. Big Picture: Three Main Layers
The search engine is structured into three main layers, each with distinct responsibilities, and all communicating primarily through Redis and MongoDB for data handling.
Data Collection Layer (Go): This layer is responsible for gathering raw data from the web. It includes the Crawler and Backlinks Processor.
Data Processing Layer (Python): This layer transforms the raw collected data into searchable and ranked information. It comprises the Indexer and PageRank + TF-IDF calculator, and the Image Indexer.
Application Layer (Node.js): This layer handles user interaction, search queries, and presentation of results. It includes the Query Engine (Search API) and the Frontend (User System).
2. Programming Languages (Core Stack)
The project leverages a polyglot approach, choosing specific languages for their strengths:
Go: Used for web crawling due to its speed and efficiency in handling multiple network requests concurrently.
Python: Employed for data processing, including indexing, TF-IDF, PageRank calculations, and image processing, thanks to its rich libraries for text, math, and data science.
Node.js (JavaScript): Powers the backend API (for user login/signup, search queries, bookmarks, and frontend integration) and the frontend, offering fast API development and seamless frontend connectivity.
3. Services and Their Jobs
Each component within the layers has a specific role:
Crawler (Spider) (Go): Visits websites, extracts text, links, and images, then saves this raw data to Redis.
Indexer (Python): Reads pages from Redis, tokenizes text into words, and builds the search index, which is stored in MongoDB.
Image Indexer (Python): Collects and indexes images extracted from crawled pages, also using Python's data processing capabilities.
Backlink Processor (Go): Stores "who-links-to-who" data in MongoDB, essential for PageRank calculations, highlighting Go's efficiency for data manipulation.
PageRank + TF-IDF Calculator (Python): Assigns importance scores to pages (PageRank) and keywords (TF-IDF), crucial for ranking search results.
Query Engine (API) (Node.js): Acts as the "brain" for user search requests, finding relevant results from MongoDB, combining scores, and sending them back to the frontend.
Frontend (Client) (HTML + CSS + JS): The user interface, providing the search bar, displaying results, bookmarks, and login functionalities.
4. Databases and Storage
Two main database systems are used for different purposes:
Redis: Serves as a high-speed, temporary data store. It acts as the "messenger," storing URLs to visit next, crawled pages before indexing, and queues for services. It's lightning-fast for short-term memory and "to-do" lists.
MongoDB: Provides permanent data storage. It's the "brain storage" or "library," holding indexed words, backlinks, PageRank scores, TF-IDF values, and user information (pages, links, scores). Its flexible, document-based structure allows for easy querying with JSON-like data.
MinIO / S3 (optional): Used for storing large files like raw HTML pages if needed, offering a solution for significant data volumes.
5. Communication Between Parts
Data flow and communication are critical for system operation:
Redis as the "messenger": Facilitates communication between the Crawler, Indexer, and MongoDB (Crawler → Redis → Indexer → MongoDB).
Node.js connects everything to the user: The Query Engine (Node.js) talks to MongoDB to retrieve search results and then sends them to the frontend.
MongoDB as the "brain storage": All important persistent data (pages, links, scores, user info) resides here.
6. Tools That Make Everything Run Smoothly
Tools for deployment, testing, and monitoring are also part of the stack:
Docker: Used to pack every part of the system into a container, ensuring portability and eliminating "it works on my machine" issues.
Docker Compose: Orchestrates all containers (Go, Python, Node, and databases) to run together with a single command.
GitHub Actions: Automates the building and testing of the code, supporting continuous integration.
Prometheus + Grafana (optional): Monitors performance and provides insights into how fast the system is running.
7. Simple Flow of How Everything Works (Data Flow)
The system operates in a clear, sequential flow:
Crawler (Go) → Redis: Fetches web pages and saves them to Redis.
Indexer (Python) → MongoDB: Reads pages from Redis, breaks text into words, builds an inverted index, and saves it in MongoDB.
PageRank/TF-IDF (Python) → MongoDB: Calculates page and keyword importance scores and updates MongoDB with these rankings.
Query Engine (Node.js) → Users: Searches the index in MongoDB when a user types something, combines TF-IDF and PageRank scores to rank results, and sends the top results to the users.
Frontend (HTML/JS) → User: Displays search results beautifully in the browser, along with other user interface elements.
8. Why This Setup Works (Architecture Benefits)
The chosen architecture and technologies offer several advantages:
Fast: Go handles thousands of web requests efficiently for crawling.
Smart: Python processes text and ranking using proven algorithms.
User-Friendly: Node.js creates fast APIs and a smooth, modern user experience.
Scalable: Each part runs independently (Dockerized), making it easy to scale the crawler, indexer, or query engine separately.
Portable: Docker allows the entire system to run anywhere with one command, simplifying deployment.
In essence, this project outlines a robust, scalable, and efficient search engine leveraging specialized tools and languages for each core function, from data collection to user interaction.
